unit.title: Use research methods to generate evidence-backed hypotheses

claim.text: The source lists analytics funnel analysis (find where to test), session replay (what is confusing), heatmaps/scroll maps (placement and reach, weighted by revenue per click), on-site surveys (objections), user testing 5-8 people (usability problems), and customer interviews (messaging hypotheses); research output is a prioritised evidence-backed hypothesis.
claim.quote:
Analytics funnel analysis (GA4, Shopify): find the step with the biggest drop and the most traffic. Feeds where to test.

Session replay: watch real sessions to see rage clicks, dead clicks, loops, form abandonment. Feeds what is confusing.

Heatmaps/scroll maps: see what gets attention and what is missed. Feeds hypotheses about placement and reach. Weight by revenue per click, not raw clicks.

On-site surveys (exit intent, post-purchase): ask why people did not buy or almost did not. Feeds objections.

User testing: watch 5-8 people attempt a task and narrate. Feeds usability problems.

Customer interviews: understand motivation, anxiety, and the words customers use. Feeds messaging hypotheses. The output of research is a prioritised, evidence-backed hypothesis, not a test itself. DRIP reports a 36.3% win rate because it pre-qualifies every hypothesis with analytics, session recordings, and heatmaps before building; teams that test without research see lower win rates.

unit.title: Amazon's 2000 DVD price test is the cautionary case

claim.text: Amazon's September 2000 DVD price test tested discount levels of 20% to 40% on 68 DVD titles over five days; after customers compared notes and backlash followed, Amazon refunded 6,896 customers an average of $3.10 each (about $21,377 total); Bezos said they never tested and never will test prices based on customer demographics and called even that a mistake because it created uncertainty for customers.
claim.quote: Amazon's September 2000 DVD price test is the cautionary case: per Amazon's own statement it tested discount levels of 20% to 40% on 68 DVD titles over five days; after customers compared notes and backlash followed, Amazon refunded 6,896 customers an average of $3.10 each (about $21,377 total, ABC News, September 29 2000), and Bezos said "we've never tested and we never will test prices based on customer demographics... even that was a mistake because it created uncertainty for customers."

unit.title: Client-side testing risks flicker and payload; server-side avoids flicker but needs engineers

claim.text: Client-side testing runs in the browser via JS/DOM manipulation, letting marketers own it and ship fast, but risks flicker, adds JS payload and slows the page, is easier to break, and its logic is public. Server-side testing lets the server or edge decide the variant before render, avoiding flicker, being faster, robust across devices, able to test backend logic, and working with feature flags, but needs engineers and a deploy cycle, costs more, and is slower to ship.
claim.quote:
Client-side: runs in the browser via JS/DOM manipulation. Pros: marketers own it, visual editor, fast to ship. Cons: flicker risk, adds JS payload and slows the page, easier to break, logic is public. AB Tasty: flicker "is caused by the basic client-side operation of A/B testing solutions that apply a JavaScript overlayer during page loading" and there is "no miracle fix."

Server-side: the server or edge decides the variant before render. Pros: no flicker, faster, robust across devices, can test backend logic (pricing, search, recommendations, checkout), works with feature flags. Cons: needs engineers and a deploy cycle, higher cost, slower to ship. GrowthBook: server-side "avoids any issues with flickering that can happen with client side testing."
